subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the cuts proposed in the Progressive Conservative Budget brought down in May 1985 are a direct contradiction to the commitment made by successive Federal Governments to fight poverty in this country. As a result of Conservative measures, the poorest in this country will be losing income and paying more taxes.
Mr. Speaker, we need only analyze the impact felt last spring when the Progressive Conservative Government gave away nearly $2 billion to the oil multinationals. We need only analyze the $500,000 capital gain exemption offered in the May Budget, to realize that this Government is giving to the rich and taxing the poor.
Mr. Speaker, how is it that in 1985, after so many years of debate aimed at establishing a system of social justice that would be fair to everyone in this country, that we should now have to discuss cutbacks that are entirely unacceptable to Canadian families? The Budget is proposing a significant change in the way family allowance payments are distributed. The Government's contention that these changes will increase amounts received by low-income families is incorrect. In fact, most low-income families and all families on modest incomes will be receiving less than they are receiving at the present time.
Families that are most in need, that is, those who are living below the poverty line, will be receiving less in 1986, while the rich-and I am not referring to people like some of my constituents who have a duplex where they use half as their own residence and rent the other half, they are not going to
benefit from this capital gains exemption-while the rich, and I mean those who own land for speculative purposes, and those who own apartment buildings, these people will be able to take advantage of the capital gains tax exemption, while our neediest families will have to suffer the consequences of having their purchasing power reduced and having less money to spend on essential needs. The vast majority of these families, including many families living below the poverty line, stand to lose substantial income because of the series of measures proposed by the Conservative Government.
Mr. Speaker, in the May Budget it was announced that the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption would be spread over five years, and the resulting spate of tax planning we are seeing is very discouraging. In fact, call a real estate agent today to ask whether there is any good income property on the market, and the answer will be no, because everyone is waiting until 1988, 1989 or 1990 to take advantage of this measure. And such measures will not create jobs.
Today, the Government wants to cut the average income of our families by deindexing family allowance payments. Families with an income of $15,000 in 1986 will lose $1,879 in income over the next five years, while a family with an income of $35,000 in 1986 stands to lose $3,452 during the same period. By adding tax increases to cuts in the amounts provided under the three family allowance programs, the Conservative Government has created an untenable situation for many Canadian families. Furthermore, since on the whole, the Budget measures tend to benefit rich Canadians, a family with an income of $80,000 in 1986 will suffer a loss of income of only $1,125 over five years. The poor stand to lose $754 more than the rich. Families on modest incomes will be losing over three times as much as Canadian families that are well off. [English]
The Government began by the deindexation of the pensions of our senior citizens, a most vulnerable group. Yet with the Liberals' influence and persistence the senior citizens of our great nation were able to speak aloud and defend themselves. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) said it is the family and a commitment to community which guarantees stability in our social fabric. He further stated, "it is my role as Minister of National Health and Welfare to put forward signals and initiatives which will strengthen the role of the family and give it more prominence in society". Let me ask this, Mr. Speaker. How is a family to be strengthened under already tight allowances? They are struggling now, and to further decrease their allowance will only create more problems. We all know that family breakdowns are generated

mainly because of financial problems before all else. It is unworthy and unacceptable for the Government to reduce the deficit at the expense of the nation's families, our children. With the many alternatives available to the Government, Members opposite should carefully re-examine this approach to reducing the deficit and begin to tax the rich, as they proclaimed they would do in their May Budget.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government, with its misleading rhetoric, is trying to hide the fact that, for instance, by 1990-91, Canadian families will be receiving $55 million less in family allowance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, that is why this morning, I rise in the House to protest against this measure.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Last May 23, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance, the Hon. Michael Wilson, tabled his Budget in the House of Commons. An adjustment in social programs was one of the measures announced. Mr. Wilson said this in his statement: "When resources are increasingly limited, we must also adjust social programs so that benefits are targeted to those most in need and funds are freed for other social priorities".
Well, these adjustments will be made through Bill C-70. I agree it is a partial response to suggestions made by a great many citizens, social interest groups and the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
Obviously all such groups will always ask for more money to help underprivileged people and try to better living conditions. We understand that and we share this concern for social justice. Still it does not mean that they are against opposed to our social policy readjustment and reorganization program, especially if it is to benefit very low income Canadians.
The situation of families with children is in constant evolution and programs designed to help them cannot always be geared automatically to their changing condition. Hence it does become necessary to revamp such programs now and then, and that is the purpose of Bill C-70. We believe our approach to be realistic and fair.
Mr. Speaker, our system is basically sound, but this Bill attests to our intention of fine tuning it and making it even better. We are not advocating radical changes, only slight alterations to improve the product.
For the benefit of the House I should like to recall the principles which guided us in our consultations and which are reflected in this measure.
The main objective of the review of the child benefit system we have undertaken so far is to define and upgrade programs, the better to meet the needs of Canadian families and of our
society. One of the most significant aspects therefore is to ensure that benefits and tax incentives will help those who need it most, particularly low income Canadians. For example, a family with two children under age 18-let us say they live in Ontario-with an annual income of less than $20,000 will have a net increase of $328 in yearly benefits between now and 1989, whereas a similar family whose annual income is $60,000 and therefore among the fairly well-to-do will see its benefits drop by $284 over the next three years.
It is patently clear that our aim is to help the most needy.
The second objective of the Bill is to maintain the principle of universality. I should like to emphasize that, in keeping with the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, universality remains the basic principle underlying our social security net. Family allowances are a secure source of benefits for families with children and our Government is there to help them.
Our friends opposite make disparaging remarks about those changes, but what did they do? Between 1974 and 1984 the Liberal Governments cut expenditures for social programs down from 50 to 43 per cent of total public outlays-a one-year temporary suspension of indexation in 1976, a monthly reduction of family allowances from $25.68 to $20 per child in 1978, elimination of the $50 tax reduction then applicable to each child, reduction of the child tax exemption for youngsters aged 16 and 17, and the 1983-84, 6 and 5 per cent ceiling on family allowances indexation and the child tax exemption which was announced in 1982.
Mr. Speaker, the previous Government also made changes in the family assistance system, changes which were much more radical than those we are now suggesting. If family allowances had been fully indexed to the increase in consumer prices since 1976 without interruption, they would amount this year to $51 a month compared with the current figure of $31. When they were in power, the Liberals therefore caused a loss of $20 a month for Canadian families.
Some people sometimes become demagogic at the expense of low income Canadians. Last summer, I saw the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) on television. He was speaking about our poor little children and showing boxes of baby powder. Maybe the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie lacks experience in this field. Perhaps he is not yet a grandparent, but for my part, I have seven grandchildren and I can tell him that baby powder is out of fashion and is even considered bad for babies.
I said earlier that this Bill brings about a readjustment made necessary not only by our economic situation, but mostly by the very serious difficulties in which many low income families find themselves. I would add that this is the first step in a new direction.
September 30, 1985

I can but refer to the recent report of the MacDonald Commission which pointed out many weaknesses in our family assistance system. What did this Commission suggest? In addition to recommending the elimination of present child benefits and the establishment of a guaranteed annual income, the Commission presented two options which are similar to what we are proposing. These are benefit readjustment formulas aimed, first, at providing maximum assistance for low income families and second at protecting poor families through a reduction in Government expenditures. This is very close to what we are suggesting and what will be the purpose of our reforms.
The Opposition argues that the measures in this bill are regressive and hit poor people harder than the well-off. I would like to remind the Elouse that this bill is only one component of a package proposed by our Government to reform the Canadian child benefit and taxation systems.
As concerns child benefits, the child tax credit will be substantially increased in coming years, which will be of further assistance to needy families. In addition, the reduction of tax exemptions for dependent children will benefit these same people rather than the rich.
Hon. Members will recall that measures were announced in the Budget last May to bring more equity and objectiveness to our tax system, such as the implementation of a minimum personal income tax beginning in the 1986 fiscal year. Second, there will be a temporary additional tax for high income taxpayers and big businesses. Third, there will be a capital tax for financial institutions, including the major banks and trust companies. There is therefore no question of regressing, but rather of progressing towards a more equitable system.
For us, Mr. Speaker, a family policy does not consist simply in a cheque at the end of each month for the welfare of a child. It is much more than that. Jobs for the father, the mother and the children leaving school are really what matters. Fortunately, our economy is showing signs of vigour. Over the past year,
284,000	jobs have been created by our Government. The unemployment rate, which reached 11.6 per cent in September 1984, is now down to 10.3 per cent. In the Eastern Townships where my riding is located, the unemployment rate went down from 10 per cent in July, 1984 to 8.1 per cent in 1986. Interest rates have decreased by 2.75 per cent since September, 1984 and are now at their lowest level in seven years. That is a positive record.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude my remarks by saying that the time has come for us to give a new direction to our social policy for Canada. It should be based on our country's economic recovery. That was the underlying philosophy of the Wilson budget introduced last May. By adopting this budget, the House gave its support to changes. The time has come to implement the proposed measures and to act for the benefit of all Canadians. That is the reason we should act now, Mr. Speaker. Canadians voted for change last Septem-
Family Allowances Act
ber, and I wish this Bill to be sent to the legislative committee for a detailed study.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak against this Bill. I am speaking in defence of all the children of Canada, including my 10 grandchildren. If any Hon. Member suggests, because he has fewer than 10 grandchildren, that I have a conflict of interest, I will point out that he has an equal conflict of interest.
One might call this Bill hate literature against children. This Bill, plus other budget measures, cuts hundreds of millions of dollars from the effective income of families who are raising children.
A typical family with two children and two income earners-which is becoming more common-is likely to lose approximately $2,000 by 1990. Let us look more closely at some other examples. A family earning $10,000, while receiving $79 more in benefits next year, would pay $37 more in tax. Therefore, it would have $42 more. However, by 1990, it would have less in benefits, would pay much more in tax, and would lose $280 altogether. The same picture applies to a family earning $20,000. However, a family earning $80,000 will receive $141 next year and $1,708 in 1990.
We can look at it another way. Family allowance in 1985 is $375. In 1990 it will be $404, an increase of $29. The child tax credit maximum benefit is now $384 and it will go up to $550, an increase of $156, less than $200 altogether. But the chjld tax exemption will drop from $710 to $404, a drop of $306. In other words, families will lose 50 per cent more than they will gain. The net loss will be 50 per cent.
Let us look at it another way. On these benefits and taxes a family earning less than $10,000 a year by 1990 will perhaps come out to the very same income now less $3. A family earning $10,000 will lose $35 if we reckon 1990 money in 1985 dollars, taking account of inflation.
At $20,000 in 1985 dollars, a family will lose $199. At $30,000 a family will lose $530; at 40,000 a family will lose $486, and so on. Families will lose, and these are families raising children. It is an attack on children. It is an attempt to go behind the progress made in the last two centuries. During that time we had to counteract the effect of the market system. In pre-modern times, families recognized responsibilities within the family and communities recognized reciprocal responsibilities within the community. Nobody was considered absolutely alone, fending totally for himself or herself at whatever age.
Now we are getting into a new scene. We now have a scene in which, for a couple of hundred years, the market overtook nearly all those relationships, nearly everything was marketable and the poor, the women and the children were downgraded, in fact degraded. There was a fight against it. First, child labour was prohibited in the mines and in the mills. Free

September 30, 1985
Family Allowances Act
schools were established because it was found necessary for the nation that everyone have schooling.
Since World War II, family allowance has been based on the principle that everybody, regardless of prosperity, should have an agreed minimum amount. Families who are raising children should not be forced to live at a lower standard than childless families.
We have now had another attack in the last several decades on the principle established to make veterans happy when they came out of the Forces in 1945.
The business elite has attacked, first through the Liberals and now through the Conservatives. In 1945, the family allowances program was established. In 1947, it was made universal when its cost was only 22 per cent of the federal expenditures, the same percentage as it is now. At that time it was 7.7 per cent of the federal expenditures.
Over the last 20 years, payments have been seriously cut. The Liberal Government, through the then Minister of Health, Mr. Munro, together with the Finance Minister, now the Leader of the Liberal Party tried to cut payments by reducing all payments to anyone earning more than $10,000 in the family income support plan. That plan was blocked by the 1972 election when the Government lost its majority and, with the NDP, the Government was obliged to double family allowances. Since then the Government cut back again, by about 20 per cent in 1974. The Liberals again made cuts indirectly through selective child tax credits in 1978. Then, in 1982 and 1983, the Liberals cut back still further with the six and five program, as the previous speaker has reminded us. By 1984, as a share of Government expenditure, the family allowance was cut to 2.4 per cent instead of 7.7 per cent. Now we have the attack by the business elite through the Tories. We have a Budget which, through sales tax on gas, other energy products, health products and other basics of family life, will cost every family about $1,000. What is being taken out by a shovel is being put back with a teaspoon for show.
Also, the Government has cut back on social housing, which is needed by the same families. Almost all families requiring social housing are raising children, and it is about to increase those rents by 20 per cent. It cut the money for planned parenthood. In fact, it will be saving on family benefits, directly and indirectly, $130 million in 1986 and $600 million in 1990. That money is being taken from families with children.
The cost is supposed to be too great. In fact, the cost is less than $2 billion when we consider what is paid out and what is recovered in taxes. The Government wants to take $2 billion from families but is eager to give $ 1 billion in fresh tax rebates to oil companies and $1 billion to the richest investors in a bank which went broke because of its greed and the greed of its investors. This is an anti-child Government leading an anti-child business elite. It is cutting family allowances, education, health and social housing. At the provincial level, Conservative Governments, such as in Ontario, are supporting indirectly adult only apartments.

They do not want anyone with children to live in many of the new apartments which have been built in the last dozen or so years. Both the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party blocked any attempt in the Ontario Legislature in past years to correct that discrimination against children. The message from the Government to the women of this country is that it will cut back on family planning programs and that once they have given birth, they are on their own. It says to these women: "Don't come to us for help because we must give the money to the banks and oil companies; there is not enough left for children".
In conclusion, 1.2 per cent of the Gross National Product for 1974 went to family allowance. Today, before these cuts, it is .57 per cent of the GNP, and the Government wants to cut it even further. Shame on it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on the deindexation of family allowances. As my colleagues before me have indicated, particularly those in the Opposition, this particular measure will have some very serious effects upon the livelihoods of many young children. This particular measure cannot be looked at in a vacuum. We must remember some of the measures which came down in the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) which were equally harsh. Collectively, they indicate to Canadians that the measures will be devastating.
For instance, we will have increased consumer and gasoline taxes, notwithstanding the fact that there will be a deindexation of family allowances. There has been the imposition of taxes on health goods. Of course, there was the attempt of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to deindex the old age security. However, because of the fight on the part of Her Majesty's Official Opposition, they have backed down. Also there is the erosion of the family benefits package, which will result in less benefits by 1990 to low and middle-income families.
Our official critic with regard to social programs outlined in great detail the ways in which these cut-backs will affect average Canadians and average Canadian families. However, the hypocrisy of the Conservative Party of Canada seems to be appalling. It was not all that long ago that the Conservative Party ran advertisements in newspapers. Its members advertised en masse, at the expense of the Conservative Party of Canada. I will refer to one particular newspaper article which reads: "You have heard a lot about the Constitution lately, but how much have you heard about deindexing?" That ad goes back to 1980. They seem to have forgotten, or perhaps they have not. Maybe the true, classic philosophy or ideology of the Conservative Party is taking over the Chamber-the rich get more and the poor get less. That is very evident in numerous
September 30, 1985

measures which have been put before the House. The Budget in May, and prior thereto the November economic statement of the Minister of Finance, suggest to our Party-and I think very clearly to many Canadians-that the Conservative Party believes there is no room in the country for weak individuals.
Why else would it viciously attack our senior citizens in the deindexation of their money? Fortunately, because of the opposition Parties and because of the strong will of our senior citizens, this measure has been curtailed. I have said in the House before-and I will say it again-that that was the first attempt against senior citizens, and I suggest that the Conservative Party will try again, when the opportunity arises, to implement deindexation for our senior citizens.
Now we have a deindexation proposal for family allowances. Unfortunately there are numerous Canadian families who use that money to buy the necessities of life. There are certain individuals, to whom the Prime Minister refers as bank presidents, who receive sums of money under the Family Allowances Program which they do not need. However, there are literally thousands of young families who purchase the necessities of life with their family allowance payments. In the wintertime those cheques are used to purchase such articles as boots, snowsuits and a whole host of necessities. Hon. Members of Parliament, whether they be Conservative, Liberal or NDP, would not want to begrudge young children that income in order to purchase such goods. Some families use family allowance for investing in the education of their children, whether they attend post-secondary institutions or training schools; some of the money may be put away for that sole purpose. What is the Conservative Party doing as a national Government by saying to young families that they will no longer be given that opportunity, that family allowances will be decreased because it needs to rid itself of debt? The Government ought to have thought about that when it bailed out the Canadian Commercial Bank. We are led to believe that an audit was requested by the chartered banks with regard to the money which was thrown into the CCB, and that was denied. Yet, the Government has the audacity to come before Parliament and to say that it wants to reduce the deficit by taking away money from the Family Allowances Program.
Surely the Government could have attacked some other area in its efforts to save money for the Canadian taxpayers. What about the billions of dollars which have been given in relief to the multinational oil companies, Mr. Speaker? Would it not have been better to deny that relief, instead of denying benefits to young families? Perhaps the Government could have looked at the capital gains exemption. Billions of dollars will be lost to the national treasury as a result of the implementation of the capital gains exemption which is afforded to the rich in this country. This is another example of where money could have been saved to reduce the deficit. But collectively, as a Party and as a Government, they have singled out families in this country to bear the brunt of reducing the deficit, and thus they deny, in my view, young families and young children, and some not so young, an income that they had become accus-
Family Allowances Act
tomed to having. Some Hon. Members suggest, either implicitly or indirectly, that sometimes this money is not used for beneficial purposes. There is no question. There may be some abuses. But does that mean the entire system should be destroyed? I say quite frankly that that is not the way the difficulties should be resolved.
Many families have learned to depend upon family allowance payments. Notwithstanding the gross family income, many women in particular depend upon family allowances in order to exist in what could be a very difficult economic life.
I could go on at length and indicate to the House where I think other cuts could take place in order to save money, but I think it is fair to say that when a national Government selects families to bear the brunt of its total incompetence, whether it is its dealings with the Canadian Commercial Bank, its placing of a million tonnes of tuna on the shelves, or with regards to the bail-outs of the multinational oil companies, that incompetence, in my view, should not become a burden to young families. Many members of our society, and particularly young people, are in desperate need of financial assistance. 1 would urge Government Members as well as Cabinet Ministers to review this measure which will have such a devastating effect on Canadian families.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to make a few comments in regard to the Bill that is before us. I had not really intended to get into this debate, but in listening to the comments of the opposition members this morning which compared this Bill with the bail-out of banks and rotten tuna, I think it is timely that someone put the matter into proper perspective.
In the few moments I have I will not engage in the suppositions that have been advanced here this morning, namely that by the year 1990 the net revenue to a family with children will be something less than what it is today and by the year 2000 it would be literally impossible for a family to make a living. My hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), says that the children will be back in the sweat shops and in the salt mines by the year 2000 if we keep going the way we are. All of us here know, of course, that that is not so.
What this Bill attempts to do in order to maintain the concept and principle of universality is to use the tax Act, which of course is already arranged in such a way that the rich pay a little more than the poor on a graduating scale, to use scarce public resources to help those who are in greatest need of this kind of help. My friends say that families put the family allowance away in a savings account to help their children or their grandchildren obtain a proper education. People in the higher income tax brackets, with greater disposable income, have other ways of doing that through family trusts. Parents or grandparents can put money away for children in a family trust and thus get some tax concessions. People in the lower income tax brackets do not have sufficient disposable income to create these trusts. Therefore, that argument does not wash.

What we have to look at is the fact that we have accumulated over the last 15 years of Liberal socialism a debt of $190 billion. Over the last three years the current account deficit grew by 25 per cent a year. The problem with universality is that if it is continued in the same fashion as it has been, particularly over the last three years, not only will family allowances be threatened but so will the unemployment insurance fund, old age pensions and everything else. The only real way we have to guarantee and to enhance these social programs is to make sure that the economy on which we rely to pay for these programs is healthy and is restored to its former dynamism and health.
How is that done? When things get tough, those who are in greatest need are helped, and that is what this Bill attempts to do.
I look at these social programs in two ways. The unemployment insurance fund and the Canada Pension Plan are programs to which people contribute during their working lives and which will help them when they are in need, that is when they lose their jobs, have to make a transition from one job to another or when they reach old age. We pride ourselves with having one of the most advanced social programs in the world. That, of course, is a myth but it is only a myth because it is in its starting phase. I compare social programs with those of some of the European countries. Bismarck started the old age pensions program in Germany in 1871. The program, which is much more generous than what we have presently and what we hope to have once the Canada Pension Plan becomes mature, has survived two major depressions and two world wars, and people are infinitely better off in their retirement years than they were during their working years. That is, I suppose, responsible management.
We began thinking about pension plans in the Diefenbaker years, but it was not until 1965 that we started the Canada Pension Plan. It will take until the year 2005 or 2010 before that particular program has reached its full value and maturity. In other words, people have contributed to it all their working lives and should therefore be entitled to adequate income in their retirement years. Thus, we have to do something in the meantime, which is where the old age pensions and the guaranteed income supplements come into the picture.
No one has contributed to the guaranteed income supplement or to the old age pension programs. That comes directly from general revenue-

Mr. Speaker, the amendment with respect to a six-month hoist is not nearly long enough when a Bill such as the one before us is concerned. I appreciate that if there were a last minute conversion on the government side and it decided to support the amendment, the Bill would die on the Order Paper. Although, knowing the Conservatives, I think they would probably bring it back in again at a later date.
Since the establishment of the first social programs in this country, the attacks on them have started the very next day. That has been the history of social programs in our country. It does not matter at all whether we are speaking of old age pensions, medicare, hospitalization, unemployment insurance or worker's compensation. There are those in our society, usually the well-to-do, the organized and the powerful, who
September 30, 1985

start attacking them. Even Governments which institute social programs attempt to erode them, whittle away at the benefits and try to bring into disrepute the fundamental purposes of the programs. With medicare, there is extra billing. Medical care and hospital premiums now amount to a sum of almost $700 per year for a family of four in Ontario, which is the richest province in Canada. These attacks do nothing more than whittle away at the accessibility and the universality of measures such as medicare and hospitalization.
We went through bitter experiences in this regard in Saskatchewan for all too many years. However, we went ahead anyway and saw them through. Every time we have had Liberal and Conservative Governments in this country nationally-which is the only kind we have had-they start something which they then attempt to undo. I think the Liberals have a lot of nerve. In 1970, just two years after Mr. Trudeau took over, they sought to wipe out family allowances completely and replace them with an income test called the family income security plan. That is a plan which would enable the Government to snoop into everyone's affairs. The Family Allowances Program is universal. Those in higher income brackets will have family allowance benefits taxed back and then some. The process is a great deal more efficient in this way. With a little restructuring of the income tax system, this tax back could be all the more certain.
The Liberals wanted to wipe out the family allowance. I am glad to see that they have been converted, although I suspect the conversion will last only as long as they are in opposition. They are notorious for being great progressives when they are in opposition. However, as soon as they are in government they revert to the traditional conservative style of governing and the traditional conservative attitudes toward social programs. It was only when there was a minority Government from 1972 to 1974 that we were able to force the Liberals to abandon the family income security plan. I must say that at that time the Conservatives were just as vociferous as we were that there be no tampering with the Family Allowances Program. The Conservatives and the New Democrats fought together at that time and we won that round.
The faces have now changed but the speeches have not. We have had Liberals stand up in the House and make the same speeches which Tories made in those two years. We have Tories standing up and making speeches which the Liberals made during that period of time. That is something which has occurred a great deal since last September 4. It is pure hypocrisy to hear the Liberals defending the principle of universality in social policy given their record in office. A former Minister of National Health and Welfare, John Munro, assailed universality, while his Cabinet colleague and Minister of Finance at the time was none other than the present Leader of the Opposition. How much credibility do they think they have?
Much has been made about the national debt and the ability of the country to afford family allowance benefits. In 1974, the interest on the national debt was 22 per cent of all federal expenditures, the same percentage as now. In 1947, some 7.7
Family Allowances Act
per cent of federal expenditures went to family allowances. In 1984, some 2.4 per cent of federal Government expenditures went to family allowances. The last major increase in the program occurred in 1974, due to the fact that a minority Government was in power and we forced the Government into making the increase. From 1972 to 1974 family allowances were doubled and indexed, which accounted for only 6.1 per cent of federal expenditures. Today, they make up 2.4 per cent of Government expenditures.
The National Council on Welfare has pointed out what deindexing will mean to families on low incomes. The council has pointed out that those in the $9,000-a-year or less range will lose money. There are many Members in the House with families in their constituencies who fit into that category.
I do not understand the Government now after its many years in opposition-and I have been here for almost 17 of those years. The Conservatives joined with the New Democratic Party to fight the efforts of the Liberal Government to whittle away and destroy universality. But now they do not believe in universality. It seemed then as if the Liberals thought that the old age pension would destroy incentive to work, just like the Tories do now. It does pay to be consistent, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to one's own basic principles, as well as the principles of a political Party. If the Conservatives had stood up in the debate on this Bill and said they have changed their minds and admitted they were wrong, their credibility would have been improved. If they had said that they were wrong in the years in which they fought the Liberals to get those family allowances indexed, if they had said they now agreed with the position the Liberal Party took a number of years ago, then there would be some semblance of honesty in the position taken by both Parties.
We welcome the Liberals who joined with us in fighting to preserve full indexing for family allowances, just as we did when the Conservatives joined us in supporting full indexing. But I wish the Conservatives would be straightforward and tell us honestly and openly that they have changed their minds, that they were wrong before. But, of course, Mr. Speaker, all they have done is to change positions, and there is nothing new about that. The only difference between the Conservative Party and the Liberal Party is that one is in and one is out. In fact, Mr. Speaker, both Parties notoriously and historically have taken money from the rich and votes from the poor, and then promised to protect them from each other. Surely a kind of straightforward honesty is needed from both the Government Party and the Liberal Party. The Conservatives should have the courage to stand up and say, "We've changed our minds. We want to do what the other fellow wanted to do before". If they were honest about this, perhaps they would receive a little more credible treatment from the people of Canada.
I hope the House will decide at the eleventh hour to support the six-month hoist, and that will be the end of that. The Government can come back with a host of other means which

The Conservative Government was elected with a large majority by the people of Canada who asked us to give them a better administration and that is exactly what we are doing at this time.
My riding of Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine for the past 22 years under what we called Liberal despotic rule. My riding has one of the highest rates of unemployment in the country and we have seen the full gambit of Liberal programs. Every now and then we listen to a member of the New Democratic Party criticizing the Conservatives but providing no better answers than the Liberals had. We can never forget, Mr. Speaker, that the economy must go hand in hand with our social programs. When our pockets are empty, we cannot buy food, and this is the dilemma we are in now in 1985. This is the great heritage left to us by our Liberal predecessors.
Being a young politician and a young man with four children, I realize that with our country' national debt, my children and their children will not be able to survive on our present programs. This is the reason the Government has taken these steps. When the Opposition cries that the poor people are not going to get as much as they already receive,
this is false. Families earning less than $25,000 will receive more. The 3 per cent indexation represents 94 cents per month, which, in this day and age, Mr. Speaker, means absolutely nothing. But whether it is a family who earns under $25,000 or a family who earns over $100,000, there is no national pride, and the deeper our national debt grows, the less our national pride will be.
On September 4, 1984, we said that we would put our house in order, and that is exactly what we are doing. The old Liberal programs did not succeed. This new Government is about to change completely the national image and will once again instil a national pride in our people. Speaking on behalf of my constituents, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that the change which was made in September of 1984, was a change desperately needed and a change about which the people are proud and happy. They finally have a Government which is realistic, a Government with a good administration, and a Government which is concerned with the poor people in this land.
I trust that the Conservative Party will be in power for the next 100 years. Unfortunately, we in this House will not be around that long. However, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that with the new Government programs and with the contribution of every single Canadian, we must attack our national debt. We must all contribute, and that is what this Government is asking. I can assure this House, as I can assure all Canadians, that with good Government administration, our children, our grandchildren and those who follow will be much better off in the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make some general comments concerning Bill C-70. A previous Conservative speaker said that "our main concern is to help the needy". I have some difficulty believing that Member. I believe that Canadians generally have considerable difficulty in believing that the main concern of this Conservative Government is to help the needy, and I want to indicate why.
If one looks at the Budget of May 23 and its over-all impact, one cannot help but conclude that the Budget is unfair. It is sneaky. It is a vicious attack on the needy and the disadvantaged in our society. Before the Budget was handed down, we were told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), Ministers of the Crown, indeed all Conservative Members, that it was going to be tough but fair. Ministers fanned out across the country to tell people that it would be tough but fair. The Opposition asked for the Budget at an early date, but were told by the Prime Minister that the Government was in the process of consulting with Canadians. The Government wanted to know what Canadians had to say about the Budget that was to be handed down, but we were continually told that it would be tough but fair. I would like to ask you, Mr. Speaker, what is fair about that Conservative Budget? What is fair about a
September 30, 1985

Budget that tries to deindex senior citizens' pensions on the one hand, and on the other give a $125,000 cash bonanza to the most affluent in our society by means of a capital gains deduction? Where is the fairness, where is the equity? There was none in that Budget.
The Government recognized that the proposal to deindex senior citizens' pensions was not fair, equitable or just. As a result of the position taken by the Opposition in this Parliament and as a result of a groundswell of opposition to that measure, the Conservative Government had to back down. It had to admit to the people of Canada that what it proposed to do was a mistake. It was unfair. However, not only that measure was unfair, so is this measure we find in Bill C-70. It is an attempt by the Government to deindex family allowance payments.
In his opening comments, the Minister indicated it was the intention of the Government to give more to the needy in society and that Bill C-70 would not only do that, it would also attack the deficit. I need not say that this Government is preoccupied with deficit reduction. It is paranoid about the deficit. It is for that reason we have this Bill before us. It is not, as the Government says, to help those most in need in our society.
If we closely examine the motivation of this Government it is easy to conclude that it is motivated by debt and deficit reduction. That is why this measure is before Parliament. Well, I say to Hon. Members opposite that we in the Liberal Opposition are concerned about the deficit as well. We believe in fiscal responsibility. We believe as parliamentarians and as a Government that we must act responsibly when it comes to the finances of the nation. However, unlike the Conservative Government we believe in people. We believe in families. We believe in children. We care about families and children. This Conservative Government does not appear to care. It is quite prepared to reduce the deficit on the backs of the disadvantaged in our society. Where is the justice, where is the fairness? We in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition say, if you want to reduce the deficit, do not do it on the backs of the disadvantaged, the poor, the elderly, the young and the unemployed because we will not put up with it. We will fight you every inch of the way. If the Government is concerned about reducing the deficit, then let us be fair and just about it. If the goal of this Government is to redistribute the wealth in this society so that those most in need receive more, then let us not tinker with universality. Let us not assault the social safety net. If the Government is truly concerned about giving more money to the needy, then let us talk about reforming the tax system. Let us talk about a minimum tax on the rich.
In the last election compaign, indeed in this House, Conservative Members indicated that they intended to bring in a minimum tax. Well, here we are a year later and where is that minimum tax on the rich? Where is the fairness and equity in allowing people earning $100,000 or $200,000 to avoid paying any taxes at all? Where is the justice? There is none.
This Government believes that Government is in business to reduce the deficit. Members opposite believe that running this
Family Allowances Act
country is like running a business. You know as well as I do that the purpose of a business is to show profit. You must show to your shareholders that you are balancing the books and you are showing a profit. On the other hand, we in the Opposition believe that Government is in business to serve people. Yes, it is quite possible to eliminate the deficit overnight. We all know that. We can do that, no problem at all. Let us get rid of universality and unemployment insurance. Let us get rid of all the transfer payments to the provinces regarding health and education. If we do that, we can eliminate the deficit, no question. But Canadians do not want that. We have a standard of living second to none and Canadians have come to expect and appreciate the highest level of health care and education in the world. Canadians have come to appreciate the fact that regardless of where you live in this great country you will receive a high level of education. But Canadians do not want our standard of living to be affected.
I note that you have indicated that I have but a minute left, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this piece of legislation is regressive, anti-family, and anti-children. I hope that the Government will reconsider and withdraw this unfair piece of legislation, just as it did the proposal to deindex senior citizens' pensions. If the Government truly believes in helping the needy and less fortunate in our society, let us talk about a more equitable and more progressive income tax system.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in this very important debate. We have heard some suggestions that the Bill before us and the policy which it represents are sneaky. I suggest to you that there is nothing more sneaky than theft, particularly theft in the night. It was the previous Government that stole Canada's Visa card and ran up $8,000 of charges on it for each man, woman, and child in the country. It cannot be paid off. The previous Government would not pay it off. The interest is accumulating at $100 per individual per month and more charges were made at a rate exceeding $1,000 a year for each person in the country until the present Government took office.
This Government is determined to bring the Canadian spending spree to a halt, but not at the expense of social programs. This Bill is about fairness, not sneakiness. The previous speaker referred to some sense of paranoia about the deficit. I would ask him what he would do about the deficit. Would he monetize it? The Liberal Party was at one time interested in balancing the books of this country. Where have its morals and principles gone?
In all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, one of the difficulties which besets us is the fact that following the calamity of World War II our entire system was geared to a preindustrial society. Suddenly most western Governments became affluent and demands were made upon them in the area of invasion of the economy generally that had never been anticipated. Governments responded to those demands, the people responded to

September 30, 1985
Family Allowances Act
those who responded to their demands, and the vicious circle was compounded.
The New Democratic Party has attributed all kinds of woes to the Conservatives and the Liberals. That is awfully easy to do because the New Democratic Party has never had the responsibility of administering anything. When it does take office in other jurisdictions it is clear that sooner or later it has to face the realities of economic life. There have been some drastic roll-backs of benefits in the western European democracies which have had socialist Governments. The proposal here is not to roll back benefits, but rather, as part of a bigger package, to transfer resources to needier families. This whole package has that objective and effect. To move away occasionally from the principle of full indexation is nothing new. No Party has a monopoly on virtue in that regard. I cite the examples of 1976 and 1978 and the six and five program in 1983-84.
The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) referred to some seven, eight, and nine-year projections and predicted calamity for our nation if we proceeded along what was called an anti-family course. We are here proposing to change the structure of these benefits over a three-year period. To assume that that would go on to infinity is ridiculous. I suggest that Members opposite would contribute more to this debate if they occasionally made some constructive suggestions. I believe that among the salient achievements of this Government to date is that we are grapsing the nettle. We are taking the initiative and making hard choices for Canada, which is what Canadian people are looking for. I suggest that members of the Liberal Party and those of the New Democratic Party would benefit greatly from reading some of the wisdom contained in the report of the Macdonald Royal Commission. That commission, appointed by the previous Government, took a fresh look at some programs and has suggested constructive alternatives.
The proposals before us in Bill C-70 relate to the whole package of child and elderly benefits. Family allowances will be increased in future years by the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index in excess of 3 percentage points. That measure takes effect on January 1, 1986. The current value of family allowances is $31.27 per child per month. The child tax credit, which will be payable in the spring of 1987, will be increased by $70 per child from $384 to $454. The income threshold above which the child tax credit is phased out as income rises, currently frozen at $26,330, will be set at $23,500 and will be increased in future years by the annual increase in the CPI in excess of 3 percentage points. So it goes into taxation years 1987, 1988, and 1989. The whole principle is to give the opportunity to needier families to benefit more greatly from these well-placed and, hopefully, well-financed social programs. However, the programs cannot be well financed if we continue along the reckless binge of spending that was initiated by the previous administration.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to take part in this debate. I would like to begin by asking why it is that Governments that get themselves into financial difficulty look to the children of this
country as the target for reduction in expenditures. It is striking that this has not only happened with this Government, but has characterized Governments that have got themselves into financial difficulty for 15 years in this country.
There are two reasons for this focus. One is a sense of misunderstanding with respect to what is being accomplished by the Family Allowances Program. People in the context of this House talk about family allowances in terms that demonstrate a lack of understanding about the transfer process that is taking place through the family allowance system. They talk about it as a transfer system from rich to poor, which, of course, it was never designed to be. It was, instead, designed to be a transfer system from those families and individuals without the responsibility for children to those families which have that responsibility. In that sense, to examine and evaluate the program effectively you must look at the significance of the costs of raising children for all categories of families in our society. I think that any Member of the House of Commons who has children would recognize that the costs are significant from a financial viewpoint, but also in terms of the sacrifice of time and the commitment of energy, the process of giving of oneself to the future of your children.
I think that family allowance represents a minor attempt- we must recognize that it is minor-to balance out within our society the burden of taking on the responsibility of the next generation of Canadians. I believe it is a transfer that is badly misunderstood and the reason Governments pick out the family allowance and view it as a magnificent target when looking for ways to achieve economy.
I also believe that the second factor that explains making this the target is the sense of lack of consultation in the real sense and the lack of caring in a sensitive way that characterizes Governments with respect to the future problems of many families in our society.
With respect to the consultation process, although the Government has made an effort to talk with a great many groups about its plans for the future, that talk has not constituted a capacity to listen. Otherwise, how can it be that, at the end of the consultation process, we find that major groups that speak for people who receive the family allowance, who speak in the area of social policy in this country, find themselves completely opposed to what the Government is doing?
For instance, it has already been stated for the record that the Canadian Council on Social Development has opposed this deindexation; the National Council on Welfare has opposed this deindexation; and the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women has opposed this deindexation. The Government will have to realize that it is creating a tremendous sense of cynicism about its own commitment to consult.
I believe that its commitment is quite well intentioned and it started out attempting to reach many groups across the country. I see one of the Ministers on the front benches who has, frankly, taken a lead in that consultation process. I know that she is a Minister who has listened-not enough with respect to
September 30, 1985

certain issues such as unemployment insurance changes-and has taken the process seriously. I hope that she will be able to reach the other Ministers in the Government and persuade them to take the commitment to real consultation as seriously. I believe it represented an interesting new initiative on the part of the Government. Initiatives are only as good as the degree to which they are carried through.
With respect to family allowances, however, all six organizations that are part of the social policy reform group have recognized that consultation as a sham. It is a sham because at no point in that process of consultation did any one of these groups concerned with social policy and the social welfare of families and children in this country, or indeed any other group representing women, children or people interested in the social policy in the country, suggest to the Government that it should effectively cut the value of family allowances by 3 per cent year.
My colleague, the Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) was a member of that committee. She sat and listened to the representations made throughout that set of hearings and she certainly heard no one come before that committee to recommend a real cut-back of 3 per cent in the value of the family allowance. That is because family allowance is a critically important ingredient in the household budget of very many families across the country. These include families led by mothers in single parent situations and families characterized by low incomes. The amount of money received from family allowance is crucial to make ends meet within family budgets.
Therefore, I finish my contribution to this crucial debate with a plea to the Government. First, it is a plea to take its consultation process seriously in the future, unlike this case, and second, to request that it look at what family allowances are actually doing-transfering income from the childless to those who bear the responsibility for the future generations in this country. I ask that the Government cease this attack on the children of Canada.

First of all, I must say I am somewhat surprised at seeing the Opposition trying to delay the passage of this legislation. I get the impression it has forgotten that from 1974 to 1984, it promoted measures to cut back social programs by 50 per cent. In 1976, the same Opposition extended indexation for one year. In 1978, that same Opposition brought about cutbacks in family allowances from $25 to $20 per month per child, it reduced and finally eliminated the $50 per child tax reduction then in effect and reduced the exemption for children of 16 and 17, and finally, in 1982, that same Opposition capped indexation of family allowances at 6 and 5 per cent respectively, for 1983-84.
Their attitude is therefore surprising, to say the least, and one wonders why they now want to postpone the passage of
Family Allowances Act
this measure for six months. Mr. Speaker, I suppose it is to give them another chance, as the demagogues they are, to alarm Canadians without telling the whole story, to make people panic and to prolong the debate and waste the time of the House for no good reason. I would therefore ask the Opposition to be a little less partisan and a little more supportive of the legislative process.
To achieve social justice, this Government wants to realign assistance programs for families with children, the emphasis being on the neediest families. We could always help more, we could always cut back more. When the Opposition was in power, although its avowed purpose was to redistribute the wealth of this country, it was actually redistributing its debts. In so doing, it has now put us in a position where we owe $200 billion. This year, the deficit will be more than $35 billion, and we must consider that our measures must help the neediest families and they must also have an economic impact. That is why we are proposing this Bill.
The Opposition should realize that the best way to help our families is not by giving the money borrowed by a Government that is getting deeper and deeper into debt. The best way to help Canadian families is to reduce unemployment and give jobs to the mothers and fathers of those families.
Some 300,000 new jobs have been created over the past year. That is a positive accomplishment which is the result of our administration. The reduction in interest rates is also contributing to our job creation efforts by encouraging new investments. This is the way to help Canadian families.
Our various Ministers have indicated clearly that they were there to help Canadian families through economy-oriented measures.
The Wilson budget mentioned for instance the loans to small businesses and partnerships which will also help promote small businesses.
There have been changes proposed to the use of RRSPs. These changes are likely to have a major impact on the development of small and medium-size businesses, because the self-administered REERs had been previously directed towards national trusts companies and, through them, channelled to every large multinational or national entities, with the result that the capital and the investor were miles apart, Thanks to the Wilson budget, they will be brought closer together, so that larger amounts of capital will be made available to small and medium-size businesses within our respective communities.
That is the way our Government is planning to help Canadian families much more than by increasing by a few dollars the family allowances. In other words, we are not going to give them a fish, but we are going to teach our businessmen and families how to fish.

Not only are low-income families losing indexation of the child tax

credit, they are also being pushed into higher tax brackets. They are getting a double whammy.
Federal sales tax has been increased, which will hit the same families. Low-income families making less than $15,000 per year will lose more than $1,800 due to all these measures. Meanwhile, high-income families have been given various advantages.
A startling revelation is that advantages given to the rich will cost the Government more than the savings realized from changes in the child tax credit and in the child tax exemption. In other words, the money saved from the changes and reductions in the child tax credit and in the child tax exemption will go right across the board to the wealthy. That is what the Government calls progress.
The Government talks about new and innovative policies, but it has removed funds for security services at small airports. Who will pay the bill? Of course it will be local taxpayers. In areas where local airports are not owned by municipalities, the Government wants to sell them to the municipalities. That will be a burden upon local people in those areas. What about CMHC? subsubtopic: LEVEL OF ORGANIZATION'S FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the first day of Planned Parenthood Week, an annual public education program of the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada. The theme of this year's program is "Kids Need to Know".
As part of the week's kickoff, the Federation released the results of a Gallup poll which for the first time surveyed 15 to 20-year-olds. It indicated that only one-third of teenagers rely on their parents as the primary source of information on sexuality.
Other important sources of information for young people are their peers and school, yet only half of the schools in Canada have sex education programs. Young people have no one reliable source for this information.
The tragically high rate of unplanned teenage pregnancies and the unfortunate number of abortions which partially result from the lack of sex education are totally unnecessary.
The Conservative Government has followed the pattern established by its Liberal predecessor in cutting funding to Planned Parenthood. This year funding from Health and Welfare was cut by 12.5 per cent. 1 call on the Government to face up to its responsibilities and restore funding to Planned Parenthood to a more realistic level.

subsubtopic: RURAL ROUTE CARRIERS-CALL FOR BETTER COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Members of Parliament who represent rural constituencies appreciate the dedication and service provided by the country cousins of urban mail carriers. Rural route couriers give their utmost, in many instances at great personal sacrifice, to the rural areas they serve.
It is only fair that these dedicated people be appropriately compensated by Canada Post for this vital service to rural Canadians and for all their expenses which relate to mileage, density of the rural routes, preparation and sortation hours worked. For too long this service has been carried out at great personal cost.
While Canada Post has dramatically increased the rates for change of address and temporary redirection services, not to mention the cost of postage stamps, the rural route couriers continue to be underpaid. It is time that they received recognition for their services and economic parity with their urban counterparts.
I urge all Members of Parliament to support the Association of Rural Route Mail Couriers of Canada in their attempt to improve their conditions of employment with Canada Post.

subsubtopic: NEED FOR AFFORDABLE CHILD CARE SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the need for affordable and accessible child care services is growing in Canada as more and more women enter the labour force. Yet, as Judge Abella noted in her report on equality in employment, Canada lags far behind western nations in its provisions for child care services.
It is time to put child care at the top of our social services agenda. The federal Government needs to continue to work closely with provincial and local Governments, community

September 30, 1985

agencies, and the private sector to help develop new and creative child care services.
A very innovative and worth-while project is under-way in Scarborough to introduce private businesses to child care ideas. With the help of a federal grant, the Human Services Organization of Scarborough is holding a series of seminars throughout the city to help interested businesses establish affordable, on-site child care centres.
I applaud the efforts of the Human Services Organization of Scarborough and encourage the Government to continue to fund projects like this, since child care is an investment in Canada's future.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCED EMPLOYEE LAY-OFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last summer during the election campaign, or in the summer of 1984, we heard a number of promises, including a promise by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to recognize and respond to the special needs of Atlantic Canada for better transportation to strengthen the economic base of the entire area and to provide jobs with the transportation sector.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, what we have seen is a Government that has allowed Canadian National to do the exact opposite. It has recently announced its intention to lay off indefinitely more than 1,300 workers across the country, as well as to freeze hiring and reduce management and non-union work force. This pronouncement was made after the CN already reduced its staff complement by 1,350 workers since January.
Where are these jobs going to be lost? In Atlantic Canada, Moncton, 185 shop jobs; Montreal, 262 jobs. Where are the promises of the Prime Minister? Where are the promises of the Government to protect jobs in transportation? This Prime Minister and this Government did not believe the promises when they spoke them, and the Canadian people will make sure they realize that in the next election.

subsubtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES-SUPPORT FOR FULL INDEXATION
speechtext:
Last Friday the Ottawa Council for Low-Income Support Services demonstrated on the Hill on behalf of all mothers across Canada to oppose deindexing of family allowances. They said: "The twentieth of the month is baby bonus day. That's the day the cheque arrives, the little bit of money, that is for you, for running shoes, hairdo money or new jeans. For some of us it is the money that will pay for an extra few days of food or keep the phone from being cut off. Thirty-one dollars and twenty seven cents is not a princely sum. If we are lucky it will keep us in Kraft dinners.
The mothers and children of this country are a resource. We are the future. If we are going to be a strong future we need strong children. Strong women and children need good food and warm clothes. Not much to ask for in a country as wealthy as ours.
I am tired of the suggestion that we don't really need the baby bonus. I'm tired of it being our money they want to cut off every time there is an economy drive. I'm tired of having to prove mothers and children are worth spending money on. I'm tired of hearing how good we've got it.
Do soup kitchens and snowsuit funds show how lucky we are? Millions of women and children in poverty in this country are not having it good. These are the people who will not see their money pegged to rises in the cost of living if this Government has its way.
So we are shouting 'Raise the baby bonus or lower the cost of living. Hands off the family allowance'."

subsubtopic: REDUCTION IN INTEREST RATES-INCREASE IN EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you well know, during the last election compaign the main issues were the economy and jobs. Prior to that Canadians had suffered through three years of record high interest rates, bankruptcies, inflation, and unemployment. This month marks the Government's first anniversary in office so it is a good time to review just what has happened to the economy during this past year- the first year of a Progressive Conservative Government.
To begin with, interest rates are down. The Bank of Canada rate, the prime bank rate, and mortgage rates have all fallen by approximately 3 per cent. We now have the lowest borrowing costs in seven years.
The bankruptcy rate has also fallen. Business, individual and farm bankruptcies are down by 12 per cent. Inflation has held steady and during the past year we have experienced the greatest price stability since 1971.
Most important of all, employment is up-up by almost
300,000	jobs which have been created since the last election.
These facts speak for themselves. They may not be news, but they certainly are reality. They demonstrate that the Government has established a climate which has allowed our economy and our country to start growing again.

subsubtopic: CHALLENGE '85 PROGRAM-INCREASED STUDENT EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to commend the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), private business throughout the country, and provincial Governments for their roles in what has turned out to be an exceedingly successful summer job program-Challenge '85.
In my constituency of Edmonton South 386 jobs were created from the 171 projects funded under Challenge '85. Some $956,000 was spent to employ students in Edmonton South.
The Challenge '85 package of programs is a comprehensive plan designed to provide career-related summer employment for people moving through the educational system. The success of this program cannot be underestimated. Throughout Canada, students and employers applauded the program. 14,000	more jobs for students than last year. A total of 100,020 jobs were created this summer. This success was reflected in the youth unemployment rate which fell from 18.3 per cent in August of 1984 to 15.9 per cent in August of 1985.

subsubtopic: MEMORIAL SERVICE FOR SLAIN OFFICERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege on Sunday, September 29, to participate in the eighth annual memorial service for police and correctional officers who have given their lives in the service of our country. The names of nine officers who lost their lives since last year's memorial service were added to the Honour Roll in the Memorial Book which is located in a room in the East Block of the Parliament Buildings.
We were reminded by Dr. Allen Churchill, Prostestant Chaplin of the RCMP, that the job of our peace officers, as they are commonly called, to maintain law, order and peace in our society, is not only their responsibility but one that we all must share.
The cities within our national capital region of Hull, Aylmer, Gatineau, Ottawa, Gloucester, Vanier, Nepean and Kanata-indeed all cities and towns across Canada-are continually patrolled and protected by our well trained and dedicated police officers. Our prisons are protected by correctional officers.
As we pursue peace in a troubled world, we should never forget the officers who gave their lives so that our families, our friends, our homes and our businesses can continue to remain safe and sound.

speechtext: My supplementary is also for the Minister of Finance. I would like to ask him, regarding the Northland Bank affair, why he and his colleague, the Minister of State (Finance), decided to put the Northland Bank and the CCB in the same bag by putting them both under curatorship in the statement made in the Commons at the beginning of September.

subtopic: REASONS FOR SIMULTANEOUS DEMANDS FOR LIQUIDATION OF NORTHLAND BANK AND CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, the Minister of State for Finance and I have been concerned about this matter for a number of weeks. We have carefully watched the development of this debate in the House and in the media. It was felt that we should establish a commission of inquiry to get to the heart of some very complex issues, in a dispassionate and objective way.
In answer to the Hon. Member's question with respect to the establishment of two separate commissions, we believe there are certain common problems between the two matters which should be dealt with by one commissioner. That same commissioner can deal with the individual, specific items relating to each bank. Because there are some common problems we think it would be helpful to have them considered by one commission of inquiry.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Minister of Finance understood my question. I asked the Minister why, on September 2, when the Government announced the appointment of a curator to the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank and asked for liquidation of both banks the Minister of Finance decided to put the two banks in the same basked requesting liquidation of
Oral Questions
the Northland Bank at the same time as he was going to ask for liquidation of the CCB.

Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure I understand the thrust of the Hon. Member's question.
On September 2 we appointed curators to both banks. We had one bank put into immediate liquidation, that is, the Canadian Commercial Bank. However, because there was a sense on the part of management that there was a chance that they could find a partner for restructuring to save the Northland Bank we felt it was in the interests of the bank, as well as the country, to give them the opportunity to seek out a partner to save the bank. That has not been possible. Thus, today, we have moved to appoint a liquidator for the two banks.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I understand the very delicate position in which the Minister of Finance finds himself today with respect to the liquidation of a second bank in Canada. Because of the difficult situation which exists at this time, can the Minister assure the House that from now on he will take all his responsibilities as Minister of Finance seriously and that he will handle this case himself so that the people of the country know that it is a major problem which faces the Government and not something to be delegated to a junior Minister?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, let me be quite precise on this point. The Minister of State for Finance has been delegated these responsibilities by me. At no time have we had any differences. Every move we have made has been fully discussed and has had my full involvement with respect to the decisions taken. I take those responsibilities very seriously and I will continue to do so. I caution the Hon. Member that he should not try to put any differences between the Minister of State for Finance and myself.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am not trying to show a difference between the two. 1 have been in that position. I know how the market looks at the Government in a situation like that. I know that the Minister is facing a terrible and difficult time now. But one thing I am urging him to do, to help him, is to make sure now that the Canadian people will know that we have a Minister of Finance who is in charge, and who is in charge 24 hours a day, so that we will not see again a repetition of the disaster which has come to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, let me assure the Hon. Member and my colleagues in this House, as well as Canadians who are watching, that the

September 30, 1985
Oral Questions
Minister of Finance is in charge. The Minister of Finance is watching very closely over the things which are happening today and which have been developing over this last six months in relation to these banks. And the Minister will continue to take those responsibilities very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, my question is directed to the Government House Leader. Will the Government empower the Commission which was established today, by special legislation, if necessary, to tell Canadians who the uninsured depositors are who will receive compensation, and who are the depositors who may have bailed out early on the basis of insider information and, perhaps, contributed to this failure?

Mr. Speaker, I think if the Hon. Member reads the terms of reference very carefully, he will see that the Commissioner has a wide scope to study all aspects of this particular matter so that those things which the Hon. Member has put before the House to date will be taken into account by the Commissioner.
I should remind the Hon. Member, however, as my colleague, the Minister of State for Finance, has said on a number of occasions, there is a legal impediment to us being able to do that. I am sure the Commissioner will take that legal impediment into account.

Mr. Speaker, as my supplementary question I want to ask the Minister if he will agree that no uninsured depositors will be paid by the Government, and that its legislation on that subject will not be pushed through this House until the Commission has made its report public and has dealt with those questions?

Mr. Speaker, we have asked the Commissioner to make his report available "as soon as possible". Those are the words which are in the Order in Council appointing the Commissioner. But 1 should remind the Hon. Member that there are people who are in need of those funds. They rely on those funds for the running of businesses, their farms, and for personal expenses. That, I should say, has got to be kept uppermost in our minds in order to make sure we do not disrupt the financial markets by long delays.
I encourage the Hon. Member, and his colleagues, to deal expeditiously with this Bill when it is brought forward by my colleague.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Given the fact that the people of Canada want Mr. Justice Estey to have all of the
power and authority to get to the bottom of the Government's $1 billion fiasco with these two banks, will the Minister assure the House that Mr. Justice Estey, in the terms of reference he has been given, will be instructed to get all the information he needs, including a list of the depositors?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Commission of Inquiry, and the Commissioner, have been appointed. The terms of reference have been made public. The Deputy Prime Minister is apparently going to be answering, so I will ask him if the question of ministerial responsibility will be looked at. subtopic: REQUEST THAT POWERS OF INSPECTOR GENERAL OF BANKS BE INCREASED
REQUEST THAT POWERS OF INSPECTOR GENERAL OF BANKS BE INCREASED
speechtext:
