They say "hear, hear". What a sad week the Tories have had, Mr. Speaker.
This all sounds good on paper, but once again this Government is trying to put one over on the people. Whether it is canned tuna or the banks or any other thing, it is another attempt to put something over, slide it by, as the Government tried to do with the senior citizens. The truth is the Government is really not going to increase the incomes of the neediest families at all. In three years the child tax credit will be deindexed and this will have the effect of reducing the actual spending money in real dollars that a needy family will get.
I would like to refer to an editorial in The Toronto Star which I hope is being read by all people who have children and by all people who have compassion, whether they are rich or poor. The editorial reads:
According to the budget papers, an Ontario family of four whose income is $20,000 a year (below the poverty line in a large city) now receives a total of $1,673 in a child benefits. By 1989, the value of the benefits would rise to $1,812 under the proposed reforms. But these figures are misleading since they ignore
the cumulative effect of inflation. If it is 4 per cent a year between now and 1989, the real value of these benefits in 1989 would not be $1,812 but $1,549, actually less than they are getting now.
That is not more for the neediest families, that is less than they are getting now. Mr. Speaker, this is a two-faced Government which gives with one hand while it takes with the other. My hon. friends on the Tory benches still refuse to look at evidence like this and refuse to listen to the counsel of social services that are the most responsible and represent the poor and the needy. They do not want to hear that evidence. They want to continue to move forward with blinders and insist that they, in their wisdom, know what is best for the poor. They do not even listen to something that is in black and white in every newspaper in the land. They refuse to hear the words as the poor cry out to them.
How is this possible? Is not one of the purposes of the Government in deindexing the universal baby bonus by 3 per cent to free up more money to give to the poorer families? Is that not what the Government keeps telling us? Is that not what the tell-the-truth Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance are telling us in their reasoning? Mr. Speaker, the Government does not seem to find it easy to tell it like it really is. It hedges and blames others as the Prime Minister has been doing in the fishy tuna incident and the investigations about the banks. This Government, this Minister of Finance, and this Prime Minister cannot seem to tell it like it is because, if they could, they would tell the Canadian public that a needy family in my riding will not gain anything by the so-called increase in child tax credits because the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are going to deindex the child tax credit too so that the gains this poor family might have made will be wiped out by inflation and additional taxation which the Government is also proposing in its unfair Budget.
The Tories will gouge this poor family of four which is struggling to live on $20,000 a year by $239 by 1989. This is how the Government claims it is going to help families like this. What is more, Mr. Speaker, the baby bonus comes to the single mother in my riding, of whom I was speaking, immediately and directly when she needs it month after month and she often depends upon it as the only source of cash which she can say is hers. That is going to be reduced. It is cruel to do this to our families in need. It is shameful to try to pull the wool over the eyes of Canadians and say that deindexing the baby bonus will add money to the federal treasury which will then be used to help the poor and the needy. It is not true.
The Government says that it wants to cut the deficit so it tries to deindex seniors' pensions and deindexes our taxes in a sneaky way while spending billions of dollars on a bank fiasco and giving $500,000 capital gains grants to the wealthy. The poor, the weak, and the middle class will be the victims of the Government's financing. It is no wonder, Mr. Speaker, that confidence in the Government is rapidly dissipating.

Mr. Speaker, today we are speaking to a motion put by my hon. friend, the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith), to hoist this debate six months hence so that this measure will receive the necessary study and serious consideration it deserves.
In 1981-82, the Progressive Conservative Party published an advertisement which stated, "You have heard a lot about the Constitution lately but how much have you heard about deindexing?" It goes on to make several points which are enlightening and interesting. For instance, it states, "The less your income, the harder you get hit". That means that indexing helps those who have less income. Therefore, indexing helps those maintain their purchasing power and gives them a chance to fight inflation and fight lower income.
The ad says, "Deindexing would take away the protection you now have against inflation". That is what the Conservatives were telling Canadians in 1981. The ad goes on to say, "But while deindexing would impose the greatest economic hardships on people living on low incomes, it would mean higher and higher taxes for all Canadians living on any income". It says that deindexing would mean a massive tax increase for all Canadians. That is what the Progressive Conservatives said.
This spring I asked constituents in my riding what they thought of the Government's proposal to deindex the family allowance, the Old Age Security and family benefits, particularly the proposal to deindex the income tax table. Out of 2,733 who responded, 73 per cent said to keep the system as it is and not touch it; 10 per cent said to reduce the monthly instalments to $20; 16 per cent said to abolish the program and 1 per cent had no opinion. When 73 per cent of my constituents say that they want to keep the system, I listen.
Did the Government ask Canadians for that kind of mandate to cut indexing? They would never dare attempt that. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) said, "If I told you what I think we will do, we would never get elected". He said that it would be unbelievable for them to tell the truth.
The Government asks for trust and understanding but it deserves to be told that they are a bunch of reactionaries. They are reacting to events and God knows that there has been enough reaction. We want leadership in this country. Canadians do not want leadership about tuna issues and deindexing family allowances, they want leadership to deal with jobs and a social security system that will be maintained. Canadians do not want the Conservatives to tamper with our social security system in order to lower the deficit.
The Government promised Canadians that the deficit would not be lowered by reducing social programs. However, in a few minutes we will vote on a measure introduced by the Government to deindex family allowances. I think we are justified in suggesting that the Government is being dishonourable by using deindexing to increase its revenues.
I want to say to all Canadians who are listening that the result of a reduction in child benefits and income tax benefits between 1986 and 1990 will cost the poorest families in Canada with an average annual income of $15,000, some $1,879. Middle income families earning $35,000 a year who have two children will see a reduction in their income of $3,452. Those wealthier families earning $80,000 or more who have two children would see a decrease of $1,125.
Who was taking it on the jaw, Mr. Speaker? The middle-income people and the poor, not the rich. That is unacceptable to us. We will vote against this motion for deindexing and we will vote against this Government when it brings in such regressive measures.

Mr. Speaker, in the short time 1 have available before the Government motion to reduce debate takes effect, I would like to express my displeasure with Bill C-70 before us, which is an attempt to deindex the family allowances paid to mothers by 3 per cent per year. The effect will be to reduce money mothers have to spend on their children. By 1990, this will have reduced the actual spending power of Canadian families by $600 million. Why did it happen to mothers and children when the Government backed off on a similar proposal to pensioners?
I think it is very clear. The Government found when it was dealing with pensioners that it was dealing with an older, politically experienced, group of people. Children and mothers do not have time nor the experience to organize politically. They have other things to do. Pensioners are voters. They have long memories and they will be around for the next election. Pensioners would analyze the effects of deindexing when it came time to vote next time. Children do not have votes.
Unfortunately, this callous Government has decided that since children do not have votes, there is no one there to listen to and so the Government can go ahead and make the reduction without any thought being taken to people's special needs.
There are special needs, Mr. Speaker. In a recent report from British Columbia, it shows that 10 per cent of that province's population and 10 per cent of its children are living in real poverty. It is estimated with this change and other changes foreseen in British Columbia that fully one-third of British Columbia's children will be living in poverty by 1990.
I see your signal, Mr. Speaker. I hope the House will vote against this proposal to deindex pensions today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SECURITY ADVISABILITY OF EXTENDING SPOUSAL ALLOWANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
I am referring to the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), who is asking the Government to reconsider its intention to limit eligibility to needy widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear there is one point that must be made above all and it is that the Government has not restricted eligibility to the spousal allowance. On the contrary, it has expanded eligibility, since thanks to recent changes to the program, 85,000 new recipients will be benefiting from this allowance. 1 cannot imagine how the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie could see this improvement as limiting eligibility. The Government and 85,000 new recipients see this change as a step in the right direction and a step towards greater social justice.
Like many other social programs, the spousal allowance is not a panacea. It has evolved and will continue to do so, reflecting the changing needs of our society. I say evolve, because even in 1975 when it was introduced, the program was far from perfect. At the beginning the spouse's allowance
September 30, 1985

program was available only to the spouses of old age security pensioners who were getting both the basic old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement, provided the spouse was between the ages of 60 and 64 and the income of the couple did not exceed a set ceiling. This program had been designed to help only those low income couples whose sole source of income was the old age security benefits paid only to the pensioned spouse.
Although this new program did contribute to improve the living conditions of a category of elderly people, its promoters had excluded a fair number of destitute individuals aged 60 to 64-widows, widowers, persons living alone, and married couples, if both spouses were under age 65. Since then, however, the initial eligibility conditions have been relaxed and the program made more generous in order to better meet the needs of a greater number of disadvantaged people within our society.
First of all, in 1979, the coverage of the program was extended so that, when a pensioner died, the surviving younger spouse could continue receiving this allowance. Later, in 1985, the coverage was extended to all widows and widowers between 60 and 64 years of age whose incomes are low, no matter the age of the spouse when he or she died.
Mr. Speaker, you certainly remember that before this amendment to the spouse's allowance, there was a good time to become a widow or a widower and a bad time. If the death of the spouse occurred when he or she was 65 years old or over, the surviving spouse was eligible for an allowance. If, on the other hand, the spouse died at age 64, the widow or widower was not eligible for the allowance. We have eliminated this condition which, more often than not, resulted in disastrous consequences: in addition to being faced with the loss of a loved one, the widow or widower had to cope with a painful financial situation.
Mr. Speaker, we have eliminated this unfair situation, and I am proud of it. We have corrected an injustice against many Canadian men and women who now owe their peace of mind to an amendment to an existing program and not from a program right out of Utopia.
Since September 1985, the spouse's allowances have been made available to all needy widows and widowers between the age of 60 and 64, no matter how old their spouse was when he or she passed away. Rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that when the Government decided to grant the spouse's allowance exclusively to widows and widowers, it never crossed its mind, as the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie seems to believe, that they were more deserving than other Canadians because of their legal status.
Rather, it decided, in view of the limited resources available, to help without further ado one at least of the groups of early retirees in need. Would it be rational, Mr. Speaker, for the Government to deny help to one group it could assist, under the pretext that available financial resources do not allow it to help everyone? In my view, the Government has the moral obligation to help to the extent it can those who are most vulnerable in our society. The new measure now being the
Spousal Allowance
extension of the spouse's allowance program to 85,000 people who were excluded since its inception in 1975.
Needless to say, legislators have a difficult task. Every legislative measure has limits. Also, every social program has special eligibility criteria. Let us take for instance the unemployment insurance program. To qualify, one must have had insurable employment for a specified number of weeks.
If we look at the eligibility criteria for total or partial pension under Old Age Security, we find that a person must be 65 or older and meet certain residence requirements. There are other programs, such as veterans allowances, workmen's compensation and so on that have special eligibility criteria.
One may ask: Why do all social programs have eligibility criteria? One thing is certain, they are intended to meet specific needs, to face circumstances which Canadian men and women face in every day life such as death, disability, unemployment, old age. All social programs have different goals, but their only reason is to help persons in need. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, we would much prefer helping every person in need, but our resources are not unlimited.
The recent change in the program will cost Canadian taxpayers $190 million for the 1985-86 fiscal year and $350 million in 1986-87. To extend the Spouse Allowance Program, as suggested by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), to all low income citizens between 60 and 64 years old whatever their marital status would cost an estimated $1.5 billion. New expenditures as substantial as this are impossible in the present economic situation. This is why we cannot introduce for the moment the kind of new social benefits suggested by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to add that this Government is helping and will continue to help people who have difficulty making ends meet and who are not eligible to the spousal allowance. Indeed, these people can receive assistance under provincial programs the costs of which are shared equally by the Federal Government and the provinces. While there are still people between the ages of 60 and 64 who cannot be eligible to the spousal allowance, it still remains that, since September 1, 85,000 of them are better off than before.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SECURITY ADVISABILITY OF EXTENDING SPOUSAL ALLOWANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words about the motion which is presently before the House. During debate on the Bill which expanded the benefits under the spousal allowance program to include the individuals who are covered by the Bill, the Minister neglected to include those individuals who are over age 60 and, by circumstances or by choice, never married. The Hon. Stantley knowles has often said in this House that it is totally discriminatory to adopt that kind of attitude. What the Government is doing in essence is saying to women over age 60 that if they did not choose to live with a man in a common law relationship or to become married, that they would not be

September 30, 1985
Spousal Allowance
eligible for any pension benefits or spousal allowance after age 60. That is the major complaint the opposition has in this measure and I presume that is why the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) presented his motion to the House.
I made the lengthy argument during second reading of that particular Bill when it was before the House and I do not intend to take up too much time at this point except to point out several things. While the Government argues that it cannot afford to include those single elderly people in this measure because of fiscal restraints, I find it strange that the Government did not use the same argument when it managed to find a substantial amount of money to bail out a couple of banks. We do not know who, because the Government will not give us the information, but in effect, the Government is going to give a sizeable chunk of the taxpayers' dollars to individuals who have invested in excess of $60,000 in that particular bank to compensate them for any moneys lost over that amount. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, to be a little bit cynical, if not hypocritical, to make the argument that the Government cannot help the single elderly because it does not have the fiscal means to do it at the present time.
I would like to quote what someone once said about this:
The fact that we have 600,000 elderly Canadians living in poverty in a country as rich and bountiful as Canada, in a society supposedly as compassionate and humane as ours, is a national disgrace. The fact that this has been allowed to continue month after month, year after year, is a telling indictment of the Government. The Government is breft of ideas, drained of decency and unable to recognize the priorities which must be dealt with in this society. I know the Government has its priorities: Bail-outs of de Havilland, Canadair and Maislin; bonuses for executive officers in de Havilland and the Canada Development Investment Corporation;... We know what the priorities of the Government are. For the people who have, throughout their lifetimes, worked for and contributed to the development of this great country, there is only a promise trotted out time and time again that some day, some time, they too will become a priority.
Is it any wonder, Sir, that today we condemn the Government? We condemn it not only for its failure to introduce legislation that would meet the current needs of today's elderly poor, but also for its failure to bring about long overdue pension reform of the whole system so that we can ensure that the poverty of today will not be meted out to those who will be senior citizens in 10, 20 or 30 years' time. We must begin to come to grips with this issue and reverse what is happening.
The words I have just quoted were said by the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald), who is now the Minister of Employment and Immigration, on May 10, 1984, when she was in opposition and was levelling a great deal of criticism at the previous Government for not doing exactly what we argue the present Government should be doing today.
I know that the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands has been a strong advocate on behalf of women and women's rights. She has been a strong advocate for adequate pensions for elderly Canadians. I know she is as disappointed as we are that the Government did not include the single elderly who have never been married under the provisions of that particular Bill.
What I am really saying, Mr. Speaker, is that it is time Governments stopped saying they do not have the fiscal capability of helping people who really need it at present and that they will look into it when the economy improves. The same argument has been used for many years for not increasing pensions for those between 60 and 64 who are single and elderly. It is time this Government stopped that and said it will put an end to this nonsense, do what should be done and include those individuals in this legislation.
The Government has argued that seniors, if not collectively then certainly on a selective basis, have other Government programs available which make life a bit easier. For example, there is the rent geared to income formula for CMHC housing. However, earlier this year CMHC notified tenants in buildings it owns and operates that it proposed to increase rents this year in the neighbourhood of 10.4 per cent. In one building located in my constituency, the Main Square apartment building, the tenants have been so notified. There are many elderly people living in those buildings and that increase practically eliminates the $50 increase they got in the supplement last year. It will wipe it out. They will be no better off. In my arguments to the Minister I have said that is totally unfair to seniors. You cannot give them an increase with one hand and then take it back with the other as this Government is doing.
As well, I understand that CMHC is flying kites at this time. Under the rent geared to income program you pay a maximum of 25 per cent of your monthly income in rent. I understand that CMHC is seriously considering raising that limit to 30 per cent. This, on top of everything else the Government is doing to seniors, will devastate many of them.
Most seniors that I know of have a very hard time of it living on a month-to-month basis. When you consider what CMHC will be doing in these subsidized apartment buildings, in addition to all the other items we saw in that Budget last May, things such as increased taxes on gasoline, alcohol, cigarettes, reduced personal exemptions as well as deindexation, we estimate that in all probability this will reduce the disposable income of seniors by something like $500 a year. That is $500 a year they cannot afford to give up.
Rather than talking this Bill out so that it becomes a dead issue after today, if Government back-benchers had any sense of fair play and decency at all they would agree to refer this Bill to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs so we can hear from senior citizens. They have not had a chance to talk about what the Government is doing to or not doing for them. Why not allow seniors to come before that committee and tell us how they are living today? In that way, all Members can get a better appreciation of the difficult financial circumstances they are living in, and perhaps we collectively could persuade the Cabinet to do what is right and proper to ensure that senior Canadians who have given their lives to our country are allowed to live their years of retirement in dignity.
September 30, 1985

As I said, I am not going to take up too much time. I have said what I wanted to say. It is up to the Government and Members opposite to do the right thing by the seniors of this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Girve Fretz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SECURITY ADVISABILITY OF EXTENDING SPOUSAL ALLOWANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to make further comments on the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) which asks that the spouses allowance benefit be extended to all needy persons aged 60 to 64 who live alone, regardless of their marital status.
It gives me particular pleasure to discuss this subject on the final day of September, because in the past few days thousands of needy widows and widowers in the 60 to 64 year old age group have already received their first spouses allowance cheques as a result of legislation passed by this Parliament on June 20 and given Royal Assent on June 28.
In his first speech delivered to the House regarding this Bill on April 18 the Hon. Member, I think rather misleadingly, stated that the intention of the legislation is to limit the eligibility of the spousal allowance to needy widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64. He seems to wish to imply that the Government has introduced a cut-back in this program which, in recent years, has grown into an increasingly important vehicle for assisting significant numbers of needy Canadians in that near elderly age group. However, the Government did not limit but rather expanded the existing program to provide income assistance to all needy widow and widowers in this age group.
I believe, then, it will be helpful for the Hon. Member to recognize that no single assistance program can respond to the requirements of all needy Canadians. In a democracy social programs inevitably are designed to provide the maximum possible assistance to a recognized group of beneficiaries within the limitations imposed by current and foreseeable economic realities. Improvements are possible over time in these programs. None of them are perfect and we concede that. All Members will agree that the needs of many groups in our society are of importance and concern to us. But no Government, past, present or future, would have the economic capacity to deal with all of those needs in one single step. It just cannot be done. Everyone must have the courage to look at the situation in their time with a sense of both justice and compassion and decide where the dollars, however limited, can be spent to achieve a positive goal.
To properly appreciate the intention of this Government's new legislation in extending this spouses allowance to all needy widowed persons in the near elderly age group, I think one must first look back to the benefit's introduction 10 years ago. The spouses allowance was created at that time for the particular purpose of assisting low-income couples where only one partner had reached the age of eligibility for the OAS basic pension and the income-tested GIS. Prior to the introduction of the spouses allowance these couples had to get by on benefits designed only for one pensioner and, at best, depending on the couple's assets and resources as well as available
Spousal Allowance
income, the younger spouse might have been eligible for provincial welfare. The spouses allowance, however, when introduced, provided these couples with an income guarantee which could be compared with that available to low-income pensioner couples where both had been become eligible for the OAS basic pension and the supplement.
In 1979 the federal Government extended the program so that a recipient, or even a widowed individual who became eligible for benefits at the time of his or her pensioner-spouse's death, could remain eligible for the allowance until reaching age 65 and becoming eligible for full Old Age Security benefits including the supplement.
Nonetheless, there continued to be criticism that the program could be considered arbitrary in providing benefits to men and women who, after they had reached their sixtieth birthday, were married to a pensioner-spouse eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement who died subsequently, but not to widows and widowers who had lost their spouse before they could become eligible for the allowance. I am gratified, Mr. Speaker, that our new legislation has corrected this anomaly. We can be proud that we have gone one step further in developing the spouse's allowance program and, consequently, in extending to more Canadians the protection of Canada's on-going system of social program benefits.
I believe I should remind the Hon. Member that the extension of spouse's allowance benefits to all needy widowed individuals from age 60 to 64 was a major recommendation of the all-Party parliamentary task force on pension reform in its final report to the House of Commons during December 1983. The task force's recommendation was made, moreover, for the same reasons that I have been discussing.
I trust, therefore, that the Hon. Member can now agree that our recent improvement to the spouse's allowance program has implemented an important expansion in benefits under the program, and not a restriction as the wording of his motion would indicate. We consider that this legislation, Mr. Speaker, is an important step toward greater social justice.
Naturally, I recognize that there are other persons in need in the 60 to 64 age group who will not benefit from this initiative. Nevertheless, I believe that this improvement to the spouse's allowance is a clear demonstration of the federal Government's firm commitment to provide assistance for all needy Canadians. I can assure the Hon. Member that the decision to extend the spouse's allowance at the present time to all low-income widowed individuals in this age group was not based on any assumption that such persons are more deserving than any others simply by virtue of their former marital status. Rather, given our limited financial resources, it was felt that we had to immediately improve assistance for at least one segment of Canada's near elderly population who have been facing severe financial hardship.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I must emphasize the commitment upon which all members of the present federal Government have agreed, to fiscal responsibility and, in par-

September 30, 1985
Spousal Allowance
ticular, to an improvement in our control of the alarming rise in Canada's national debt. I must point out that the cost of the Hon. Member's proposed amendment to the spouse's allowance legislation would be an additional $300 million during the first full fiscal year. He may be aware, also, that there have been proposals to extend spouse's allowance benefits to all low-income married couples where both partners are between ages 60 and 65. The cost of this proposal would be in the order of $820 million annually. In fact, to extend the spouse's allowance to all single and married low-income individuals in this age group would cost in the order of $1.5 billion per year. Such a drastic expansion of social program benefits that are funded from general taxation revenues is simply out of the question in light of the nation's present economic situation. That is why the level of increased assistance that the Government has determined can be responsibly undertaken at the present time has been directed to a group of Canadians who are among those most in need, namely, 60 to 64 year old widows and widowers.
Rather than lament what might be, Mr. Speaker, we should continue to do what can be done in a fiscally responsible way to help the members of our society most in need while not imposing an unfair burden on all Canadian taxpayers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to follow my distinguished colleague, the Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and participate in this second round of debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart). It is interesting to note that neither he nor any other member of the official Opposition is present for the discussion on such an important subject matter.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SECURITY ADVISABILITY OF EXTENDING SPOUSAL ALLOWANCE PROGRAM
speechtext: The real Opposition is here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SOCIAL SECURITY ADVISABILITY OF EXTENDING SPOUSAL ALLOWANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Of course, as all Members are now aware, it is not just the Government's intention to extend the spouse's allowance program to include all widowed persons 60 to 64 years of age; the Government has already done so effective September 1985. Now, for the first time, 85,000 widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64 are guaranteed a level of income which is adequate to meet their basic living costs. This group of low income near-elderly persons, like the 89,000 persons who were previously entitled to spouse's allowance, are receiving very necessary and well-deserved financial assistance from the federal Government.
I recognize that it is very easy to criticize a social program. One can always fault the program's design, its eligibility criteria, its benefit amount, and also its cost. I for one want to see more praise for our social programs, not the least of which is the spouse's allowance program. This program is a prime example. These programs have enjoyed the support of all Canadians because they are directing help where it is most needed. Let us ensure that they will continue to deserve their support by keeping social program costs at an affordable level.
Through the application of an income test, many 60 to 64 year old persons residing in this country are provided with
sufficient income to assure them some measure of comfort and security so that they can live with dignity. Mr. Speaker, the 60 to 64 year olds in receipt of spouse's allowance-the vast majority of whom are women-have supported this country in many ways over the years. In this group we find the mothers who have stayed in the home for the better part of their adult lives raising their children, caring for their sick relatives, and providing the necessary volunteer labour without which most of our community projects could not operate. This was an important role that these women played in the unpaid labour market for most of their adult lives. They depended financially on the earnings of their husbands.
These women are now widowed, and with their husband's death went the greater part of the family income. In some cases, this income had been partially protected through insurance or under private pension plans. However, more often than not, unfortunately, the widow was left with minimal, if any, income protection either through survivor benefits or through the family's personal savings. And so, what recourse do these women now have? Some are lucky and find paid employment. Very often, though, this is of the physically demanding and low paying type because these women have not had the opportunity to acquire or keep up the technological skills required in today's constantly changing workplace.
For many others, the only avenue of financial assistance is welfare. These menas and/or needs tested provincial social assistance programs are an important part of Canada's social safety net and provide much needed financial assistance to the many thousands of Canadians who are unable to provide for themselves. However, Mr. Speaker, as funds permit, I believe our elderly residents deserve special recognition, and that is exactly what the spouse's allowance program does. That is why the Government took the steps necessary to extend this income-tested assistance to 60 to 64 year old widowed persons.
I am the first to admit that there are other persons in the same age group who have given of themselves just as selflessly. However, I cannot believe that the Hon. Member who proposed this motion would have us deny much-needed financial assistance to 85,000 widowed persons because the money is not available at this time to extend the spouse's allowance program to all 60 to 64 year olds.
The step-by-step approach which successive Governments have followed in building good social programs is not wrong. If it were, then the spouse's allowance program would not have even been introduced in 1975. You remember that at the time, when the program was introduced, it was designed to protect only the 60 to 64 year old spouses of low income Old Age Security pensioner. It left out all other 60 to 64 year olds.
Nevertheless, through gradual steps, the spouse's allowance program has been improved. First, in 1978, the allowance was extended for six months after the Old Age Security pensioner's death. This extension was intended to give widows or widowers a chance to adjust to their changed circumstances.
September 30, 1985

Then in 1979, under a Conservative Government-as has been pointed out by some of my colleagues-the spouse's allowance was extended until the recipient reached age 65 and became entitled to the Old Age Security pension and its income tested component-the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
We wisk now six years ahead to June, 1985. Parliament took the next logical step when it gave its approval to Bill C-26 and extended the spouse's allowance program to all widowed persons age 60 to 64, regardless of the age of their spouse at death, thus ensuring that some 85,000 more near-elderly persons were guaranteed an adequate basic income. I think it is important to emphasize that the decision to extend the allowance to widowed persons was not just a whim of the Government. This was a proposal resulting from an extensive review of Canada's retirement income system conducted by the allParty Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform.
After carefully considering the views of all interested Parties in that pension reform debate, the Task Force recommended that the spouse's allowance program be expanded to include all widowed persons in the 60 to 64 year age category. As responsible representatives of the people of this country, that Task Force recognized it would be too expensive to extend income tested assistance to all 60 to 64 year olds, as was pointed out by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Erie. The spouse's allowance program may still not be as good as it could be, but it is better than it was prior to September. I, for one, am pleased that the Government has moved so quickly to legislate this proposal.
The Guaranted Income Supplement is another example of a social program which, since its inception in 1967, has been gradually improved. In step-by-step increments, the level of income guaranteed to Old Age Security beneficiaries was increased so that today, all OAS pensioners are assured of a monthly income which is adequate to meet their daily living needs.
Of course, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie did not suggest that we extend the income tested spouse's allowance to all 60 to 64 year olds, but rather to those in this age group who live alone. I cannot help but wonder why one's living arrangements should be added to the eligibility criteria for this program. Many people share living accommodation with relatives or friends for reasons other than financial. There are those who are not well enough to live alone and those who want the companionship and shared responsibility of living with another person.
It must be remembered that many 60 to 64 year olds live in their own homes; homes that they previously shared with their late spouses and their children. Now that their spouses have died and, in most cases the children have left home, these widowed persons are left alone to maintain, both financially and physically, the family homes.
I commend those persons who open up their homes to others. Not only do they have someone with whom to share the burdens, they are providing alternate housing arrangements to
Adjournment Debate
people who might otherwise find themselves living in a small apartment or, too often, a room.
I believe that the Government has demonstrated its sincere concern for elderly Canadians by extending the spouse's allowance program to 85,000 new beneficiaries. Given the enormous Financial deficit we inherited when the people of Canada asked us to take charge in September of 1984, it would have been justified had we said, "Sorry, we cannot help any new groups of needy Canadians. The money is just not available". However, that would have been irresponsible. We cannot and will not turn our backs on Canada's needy. We took what money we felt could reasonably be added to the spouse's allowance program and we extended the protection of this very important social program to 85,000 needy 60 to 64 year old widowed persons.
This does not make the spouse's allowance program perfect but the Government recognizes the need to make certain that Canada's needy, particularly those in this age group-spouses aged 60 to 64-do indeed live in dignity in this great country. By working together we can improve Canada's fiscal position which will in turn result in further resources for improving our social programs.
Until that time, I think we should be proud of the help that the spouse's allowance is providing, and let us not down play the importance that the allowance is now playing for an additional 85,000 low income Canadians.
The motion by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie reads;
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should reconsider its intention to limit the eligibility of the spousal allowance to needy widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64 and that it should extend the program to all persons of this age group living alone and having the same means, without taking their marital status into account.
It strikes me that even the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie and his ghostly colleagues on the other side of the House would realize that not only is this an extremely expensive proposition, but that the Government has bitten the bullet as far as doing as much as possible for the spouse's allowance and making certain that 85,000 seniors between the age of 60 and 64 who had never been considered or been eligible for this kind of Government assistance would be included.
I am proud to be a Member of a Government that has taken the spouse's allowance program this far. I will work hard toward taking our social assistance programs for Canada's needy and elderly even further in the future.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 46 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDING LEGISLATION
YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last election campaign there were many issues in my riding, but however, there were two primary issues. First was the economy and jobs, and the second was the whole issue surrounding the question of capital punishment.
In my view capital punishment is really a descriptive term that characterizes a much broader issue. That broader issue is the whole question of the adequacy of the criminal justice system at the present time. There are many people in this country who are very concerned about the adequacy of our criminal justice system and feel that it is not working. From time to time we hear Hon. Members from the Opposition say that we have a marvellous system of criminal justice that is working fine and to which no changes are needed. However, that is not the impression of Canadian citizens. That is why I believe that the whole issue of capital punishment is so substantial and why there is a great effort to bring it back after being put aside for many years.
I believe that the issue is not really capital punishment but the criminal justice system as it relates to areas such as the sentencing by judges of those convicted of crimes, the parolling of people either immediately after their conviction or after they have served some time in prison, the whole question of mandatory release of those convicted of crimes as well as the whole question of the Young Offenders Act itself.
All of these issues are part of the question the Canadian public has about our criminal justice system. If we were able to solve some of the issues that are bound up in those questions, the issues relating to sentencing, parole, mandatory release and to the Young Offenders Act, I do not think we would have the same pressure we now have from the public on this matter of a return to capital punishment.
The Government has moved in recent weeks, by the introduction of Bills C-67 and C-68, to addressing the question of mandatory release. Those two Bills have been debated in this House. They have had second reading and have been referred to a committee. The next step, in my view, toward dealing with this whole criminal justice issue is to get on with the amendments which are essentially needed to the Young Offenders Act.
A great many people in recent weeks have pointed out problems with the Young Offenders Act. An example of one of those problems arose in metropolitan Toronto a few months ago. A man who had allegedly committed armed robbery with a sawed- off shotgun was captured. While in prison waiting to be brought before the courts, he escaped custody. The individual was under the age of 18. Therefore, the police were unable to protect citizens of metropolitan Toronto by disclosing the name of the person, which would have been of help in capturing and returning him to custody. They were unable to do so because of provisions in the Young Offenders Act. That is one of many examples.
Another of the problems with the Young Offenders Act involves the whole question of criminal records and how they should be dealt with. There is also the question of young offenders under the age of 12 and how they should be dealt with.
On September 23, I raised a question in the House concerning the Young Offenders Act. I asked when amendments to the Young Offenders Act to correct all of the problems would come forward. The Minister at that time indicated he was still reviewing the matter. It seems to me the time has passed for reviewing the matter. Police departments across the country have pointed out and have identified specific problems with this Act in meetings of chiefs of police and in meetings with deputy attorneys general. Recently these problems have been pointed out in meetings of provincial attorneys general. The Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Beatty) has met with them and has heard submissions. The time has now come for action.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary tell us tonight whether the Government is now prepared at long last to introduce some amendments to the Young Offenders Act, which will set these things right and allow the police departments to protect the citizens of Canada properly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question posed by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) to the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) with respect to amendments to the Young Offenders Act, to correct issues identified by the chiefs of police and the attorneys general. He has just now elaborated further upon these problems?
In June 1985, the Deputy Solicitor General met with deputies responsible for juvenile justice to discuss key areas of concern. On that occasion, the provincial and territorial Governments identified four areas of concern: first, the requirements for predisposition and detention; second, to review provisions to assist in the enforcement of dispositions ordered by the court; third, the limitations occasioned by the ban on publication of the name or identify of a young person, and fourth, the administrative burdens and complexities occasioned by the provisions for the maintenance and destruction of records.
Since that time federal and provincial officials have been carefully reviewing these proposals for change. The Solicitor General has also stated his desire to review all these concerns and to solicit broad input.
As the Hon. Member for York East is aware, the Young Offenders Act is, for all intents and purposes, a new piece of legislation which was proclaimed in force on April 2, 1984, with the uniform maximum age provisions only coming into effect on April 1, 1985. Clearly this Act is in its formative stages. This fact is certainly evident from a number of decisions presently before the courts. As the Solicitor General noted on September 23, when he responded to the Hon. Member's question, it would be premature and indeed improp-
September 30, 1985

er to comment on matters which are before the courts and may still be subject to appeal.
Independent of these issues, however, it may be helpful to highlight the principal areas of concern. From a public perspective, media commentary has centred around the belief that the Young Offenders Act is lenient in its treatment of young criminals. Consequently, media criticism has focused upon the exclusion of children under 12; the ban on publication of names and identities; the upper age limit of under 18; and the maximum penalties available under the statute, which are perceived to protect young people at the expense of the public. From a provincial perspective, the concerns appear to focus around administrative and procedural matters. In this regard, the Solicitor General is awaiting a report of the meeting of the provincial Attorneys General which took place in Regina on September 19 and September 20.
While the concerns of citizens for public safety cannot be minimized, it is evident that many of the criticisms and the demands for change which have been advanced are the result of a serious misconception about the nature and implications of the Young Offenders Act for the administration of juvenile justice. In short, it could be said at this moment that there is no unanimity of opinion as to the problems with the Young Offenders Act, and certainly as to their solutions.
However, I should like to assure the Hon. Member that the Solicitor General is aware of the concerns of the public and the provincial and territorial Governments and is prepared to respond fairly and effectively to those concerns. In so doing, the Minister recognizes the need for countering unfounded criticisms and unsubstantiated fears about the implications of the Act, so that efforts may be concentrated on those areas which clearly require change.

subtopic: CULTURAL AFFAIRS-CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS- GOVERNMENT POLICY. (B) TIME MAGAZINE-POSSIBLE RE-EMERGENCE OF CANADIAN EDITION
CULTURAL AFFAIRS-CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS- GOVERNMENT POLICY. (B) TIME MAGAZINE-POSSIBLE RE-EMERGENCE OF CANADIAN EDITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I raised in the House last week with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) concerned the very urgent question of cultural integrity. It is a very simple question. Do we want to have our cultural industries up for bargain in any free trade negotiations? Do we really want to build Canadian culture in the country and ensure that all aspects of it have an opportunity to flourish? Do we want to ensure that jobs are kept for Canadians? Do we want to ensure that there are more opportunities in publishing, music, dance, theatre and all other fields of artistic expression?
The Government's answer has been a little two-faced. When it comes to rhetoric, its Members are quite clear. They are on the side of Canadians and on the side of cultural integrity. I am raising the questions and want very straightforward answers because their practice does not fulfil their rhetoric.
The then Minister of Communications at a conference in Halifax, in reply to questions, suggested that cultural industries were linked to other industries which would be in free
Adjournment Debate
trade talks, so they will not be exempted as clearly as they should be in any discussion of free trade. The Government's policy in Investment Canada is clear enough, that there will be exemptions for cultural heritage and national integrity. However, when it comes down to specific cases, we see that the Government does not live up to its promise.
I have raised the case of Prentice-Hall in the House, and all we have seen is delay. There has been an extended period of investigation, and we do not have any assurances. There is the take-over by W.H. Smith of the Classic book chains, which is quite unacceptable to the Canadian cultural community. It promises to have up to 20 per cent Canadian shares in the near future, but that is hardly Canadian control. It is a matter of real concern.
The possibility of a revival of the so-called Canadian edition of Time is a very troubling one inded to the magazine publishing industry. People will recall that when the previous Canadian edition of Time, of which the Canadian content was absolutely minimal and quite laughable, after a very protracted struggle disappeared it meant that advertising dollars were available and went into other Canadian publications. Indeed we saw a flourishing in the Canadian magazine publishing business. Smaller magazines increased their circulation. This was the time when Maclean's went weekly, and it has been an important news magazine for Canada.
We are very concerned that any revival of the so-called Canadian edition would not be truly Canadian in terms of its content and yet would suck off the advertising dollars that are now being spread throughout a growing and quite vital magazine publishing industry right now.
It is troubling also when we get rumours in the press of the possibility of the Prime Minister appearing at a Time sponsored event-perhaps later this fall, perhaps in Chicago, perhaps in November, the rumours are not terribly specific-that would name him on behalf of Time magazine statesman of the year.
Well, Mr. Speaker, one country's statesmen may be another country's sellout and we have to be very concerned about this kind of flattery that has been used by Time magazine in the past. We think of a former Prime Minister, Mr. John Diefen-baker, who was courted actively by Time magazine, flattered and indeed got a great deal of circulation and a great deal of press. We are very troubled to think that a Prime Minister might succumb to the gentle persuasion of a large and important mass media magazine.
The threat of the Time magazine revival is a very real one in the Canadian cultural community and I want the Government to be very clear that the arts community does not want more rhetoric. We do not want these statements of good book publishing policy which then get reversed in practice in Investment Canada and in other decisions that come up. We want the Government to be consistent and to accept the concerns of the arts community and indeed of all Canadians to build Canadian culture, and to make it strong. The talent is there

Adjournment Debate
and we want them to have the opportunity. They can only have that by having good policies that are realized in practice.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CULTURAL AFFAIRS-CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS- GOVERNMENT POLICY. (B) TIME MAGAZINE-POSSIBLE RE-EMERGENCE OF CANADIAN EDITION
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It is with great pleasure that I respond on behalf of the Acting Minister of Communications to the concerns raised by my friend, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) on the subject of Canadian cultural policy and the possible re-emergence of another Canadian edition of Time magazine.
These matters are of great interest to all Members of this House. It is very timely that the Hon. Member should bring this forth at this adjournment debate on this particular day when she will know that earlier today in Question Period the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has reiterated the very clear and unequivocal statement made by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) that Canada's culture is not an issue in any forthcoming talks with the United States relating to enhanced trade.
The former Minister of Communications, the Hon. Marcel Masse issued in his release at the close of the meeting of the federal-provincial Ministers responsible for culture in Halifax this statement:
Any trade negotiations we may enter into with any country must and will take into account the fundamental principle that it is culture that guarantees the expression of the distinctive character and identity of a people.
I stand by every word in that news release. The Hon. Member may put that down to rhetoric but not when it is stated in as clear and definite terms by the former Minister of Communications, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister of Canada. I shall give the hon. lady my assurance that I share her concerns. I am making my views known to the people responsible as we head into those very delicate negotiations.
With respect to the question of Time magazine, 25 years ago the Royal Commission on Publications recommended that Canadian publications should have better access to the advertising dollars spent by Canadian companies in Canada. In 1965, the Government amended the Income Tax Act to stop Canadian advertisers from buying ads for the Canadian market in foreign publications.
Shortly after the introduction of Bill C-58, Time Inc. decided to stop publishing its Canadian edition. This amendment of the Act meant for Time Inc. a loss in advertising revenues. Canadian advertisers could no longer deduct their advertising expenses in Time Inc. from their revenues for income tax purposes.
The return of a Canadian edition of Time involves a transaction that would transfer 75 per cent of Time Canada's shares to Comae Publications, a large Canadian publisher of controlled circulation publications, and the transfer of 25 per cent of Comae's shares to Time Inc. of New York.
I am informed that while there have been some informal suggestions made by Time that it might want to start up a Canadian edition, they are strictly informal. Time knows what it is up against. We still concur with the philosophy behind the law. We believe that the Canadian newspaper and periodical industries must evolve in a favourable economic context which will consequently guarantee the largest possible dissemination of our Canadian cultural values.
